title: Given a set of root words and a sentence, replace every word in the sentence with the shortest root that is a prefix of it, leaving words with no matching root unchanged. Explain how the Trie pattern solves it, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Replace Words with Root (Shorten Words to Their Shortest Registered Root)

s1_definition.profdef: Replace Words with Root is a prefix-matching application of the Trie pattern. We insert all root words into a trie, then for each sentence word we walk the trie character by character and stop at the first node marked as a root, which is the shortest matching root. We replace the word with that root, or keep the word if no root prefixes it. Each word costs time proportional to its length.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India normalises long transaction descriptor words down to their shortest registered root code, so SALARYCREDIT collapses to the root SAL. A trie of root codes lets each descriptor be shortened to its earliest matching root.
s1_definition.oneliner: Walk each word through the trie and cut it at the first node marked as a root.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Replace Words with Root is a prefix-matching application of the Trie pattern. We insert all root words into a trie, then for each sentence word we walk the trie character by character and stop at the first node marked as a root, which is the shortest matching root. We replace the word with that root, or keep the word if no root prefixes it. Each word costs time proportional to its length.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India normalises long transaction descriptor words down to their shortest registered root code, so SALARYCREDIT collapses to the root SAL. A trie of root codes lets each descriptor be shortened to its earliest matching root.

**One line to remember:** Walk each word through the trie and cut it at the first node marked as a root.

sections.s2_technical:
We insert every root word into a trie and mark the end of each root. To process a sentence word we walk the trie from the root following the word's characters. The moment we reach a node marked as a root, we stop, because that is the shortest root that is a prefix of the word, and we use the characters consumed so far as the replacement. If at some character there is no matching child, no root prefixes the word, so we keep the original word. If we finish the word without ever hitting a root node, we also keep the original.

The per-word core is `StringBuilder prefix = new StringBuilder(); TrieNode node = root; for (char c : word) { if (node.isRoot || !node.children.containsKey(c)) break; node = node.children.get(c); prefix.append(c); } return node.isRoot ? prefix.toString() : word;`. A concrete check: with roots SAL and REN, SALARY becomes SAL and RENTPAID becomes REN. Senior nuance: this is linear in the total sentence length plus root size, stopping at the first root node gives the shortest root automatically, and it is a classic prefix-replacement use of the trie.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India normalises transaction descriptor words down to their shortest registered root code so that varied descriptors like SALARYCREDIT and SALARYBONUS both collapse to the root SAL for consistent reporting. Matching each word against every root separately is slow. This is exactly how Replace Words with Root works: it stores the roots in a trie and shortens each word at its first matching root.

The code defines a `DescriptorNormalizeService` with `replaceWithRoots(roots, sentence)`, plus a `TrieNode`. A `Demo` runs it over a sample root set and sentence and logs the normalised sentence.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is the root set SAL and REN and the sentence SALARYCREDIT RENTPAID FEES. We want each word shortened to its shortest matching root.

Step 1 — We build the trie, marking SAL as a root along the S, A, L branch and REN as a root along the R, E, N branch.

Step 2 — For SALARYCREDIT we walk S, then A, then L, and at the node after L the root flag is set, so we stop and replace the word with SAL.

Step 3 — For RENTPAID we walk R, then E, then N, and at the node after N the root flag is set, so we stop and replace the word with REN.

Step 4 — For FEES we try to walk F, but the root node has no child F, so no root prefixes this word and we keep FEES unchanged.

Step 5 — Joining the pieces gives the normalised sentence SAL REN FEES. The output is below.

```
Oct 27, 2026 10:05:13 PM com.bank.descnorm.service.DescriptorNormalizeService replaceWithRoots
INFO: Normalised descriptor = SAL REN FEES
Oct 27, 2026 10:05:13 PM com.bank.descnorm.DescriptorNormalizeApplication main
INFO: Normalised descriptor sentence: SAL REN FEES
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Roots {SAL, REN} → trie:  root → S→A→L(isRoot), root → R→E→N(isRoot)
    │
    ▼
  per word, walk trie, stop at first isRoot node
    │ SALARYCREDIT → S,A,L → isRoot → "SAL"
    │ RENTPAID     → R,E,N → isRoot → "REN"
    │ FEES         → no child 'F' → keep "FEES"
    ▼
  Output: "SAL REN FEES"
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Replace Words with Root is a prefix-matching application of the Trie pattern, and the elegant part is that stopping at the first root node along a word's path automatically gives the shortest matching root. I insert every root word into a trie and mark where each root ends, then for each word in the sentence I walk the trie from the root following the word's characters.

The instant I reach a node marked as a root, I stop, because that is the shortest root that is a prefix of the word, and I use the characters consumed so far as the replacement. If at some character the trie has no matching child, then no root prefixes the word and I keep it unchanged, and likewise if I finish the word without ever hitting a root node I keep the original. Each word costs time proportional to its own length, so the whole sentence is linear in its total length plus the size of the roots.

At the National Bank of India I used this to normalise transaction descriptor words down to their shortest registered root code, so that varied descriptors like SALARYCREDIT and SALARYBONUS both collapsed to the root SAL for consistent reporting. I stored the roots in a trie and shortened each descriptor at its first matching root. Explaining that the first root node on the path is the shortest match, and that a missing child or no root means the word stays, is what shows an interviewer I understand this prefix-replacement use of the Trie pattern.
